#3508. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Director Francis Lawrence on the Film’s Final Scene

When Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow. “All I need is a big eagle back here,” the white-haired, smartly dressed director jokes.

Lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment. He joined the franchise for its 2013 sequel, Catching Fire, and has directed only three non–Hunger Games movies in the decade-plus since. In that time, one could argue, the world has tilted further toward the oppressive future depicted in Collins’s novels—see, for instance, Donald Trump’s Hunger Games–esque Patriot Games. And while Lawrence isn’t naming names, he’s never lost sight of the movies’ larger political message. “I feel really lucky to be able to tell stories that matter, that are wrapped in these commercial packages,” he tells Vanity Fair. “So anytime one of these things comes around, I jump at it.”

Just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the new movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada. He plays the younger version of Woody Harrelson’s Haymitch Abernathy, a victor of the Hunger Games who later serves as a mentor to actor Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen. Making a reflective movie prompted director Lawrence to reflect on his own Hollywood trajectory. “The biggest difference is that I’m a lot more relaxed. I was nervous as hell on Catching Fire,” he says. “It was my fourth movie. It was a movie I was inheriting. It was a big movie, and it was a massive cast. So I was really intimidated. Now I have much more fun, I will say. I’m much more comfortable with actors, and the amount of actors, and with logistics. And there’s definitely a family that’s built into it, which is very important for me. There’s, what, 14 years of my life spent making these movies? So it has to be fun.”

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: When did you become aware of Sunrise on the Reaping, and at what point did you and Suzanne Collins start discussing an adaptation?

Francis Lawrence: When we did the original series of movies, and we finished the last Mockingjay, she said she was done, and we thought that was it. Then she surprised me and Nina [Jacobson], the producer, with Ballad, however many years later. And she never tells us when she’s writing. Even when she has something to read, she never tells us what it’s about. She’s very superstitious about it all. So we got the call, which was very exciting. And she said, “Go to my agent’s house. There’s a manuscript. Let’s talk after you read it.”

I got to his house, sat in his backyard, and there was a manuscript and a copy of Catching Fire sitting on top of it with a few tabs in it. I opened to the tabs and saw that it had the portion where Katniss and Peeta were looking up the Haymitch Games, that sequence from the book. And I was like, Oh, she’s written the Haymitch story, which was very exciting. And that started the process that we always have, which is that I read the manuscript in one sitting, then read it a second time after having a conversation with Suzanne.

Then I fly to New York and meet her at Scholastic, and we sit up in a conference room for about a week going through the book, beat by beat, of what we think the movie is going to be. She and I lay it all out and chat, and she sits on her computer and writes a scriptment. Then that’s the thing that we turn over to the screenwriter.

How have you built that trust with the author of these books, having adapted them for more than a decade now?

That working process happened accidentally when I signed on to do Catching Fire. I had never done a sequel to someone else’s first movie before. And when Lionsgate and the first director, [Gary Ross], parted ways and I got the call, they didn’t have a script, but they had started the process of developing it before I was on board. And so I signed on based on the book and had planned a trip to New York to meet with Suzanne.

The script came on the day that I was traveling to New York. I read it, and it was not the movie that I wanted to make—because I loved the book, and it was not the book. Luckily, nobody else wanted to make that version of the movie either. Our meeting of me just picking her brain turned into, “This script doesn’t work. Let’s go through, page by page, and figure out the version of the movie we want to make.”

That’s what really formed the bond—just working really, really closely with her. Spending 8 or 10 hours a day for a week or two in a conference room—me riffing on visual ideas and her talking about the story. We think the same way in terms of storytelling, structure, and she seemed to take to my visual ideas.

There’s this weird dynamic that happens as we get closer to production. We’re usually developing the script pretty much within a week of shooting. But the production is also building. So you have thousands of people working, figuring out locations, traveling in different parts of the world. The stress levels are building.

Suzanne and I have related the relationship to almost like a mother-son relationship. It starts really lovely and creative, but then as we get closer and closer, it’s me being that late teen who’s ready to leave the home, like, Okay, enough’s enough. I’m going to go make the movie now. I have to say, I love the process. It’s not without its stress sometimes, but that’s part of the closeness of it all that I cherish.

How did this film’s futuristic-meets-1970s aesthetic come about?

There was an element [of the story] that reminded me a bit of Alice in Wonderland, which then made me think of Jefferson Airplane, that song “White Rabbit,” which brought me to the ’60s and ’70s. Then you can look at characters certain ways. Like, Haymitch, you go, Okay, he’s from, like, young Bruce Springsteen, or Lenore Dove [played by Whitney Peak], like a young Stevie Nicks. And you get this hippie vibe. And the Capitol is that Warhol Studio 54 crowd, and Snow like a ’70s Yves Saint Laurent.

How do you go about casting a young Haymitch, finding an actor who can anchor the film like Jennifer Lawrence did in the original Hunger Games film?

Our casting director, Deb Zane, had met him, and I want to say before he did East of Eden. She had a lot of faith in him. We liked his self-tape a lot. But we knew that he was going to have to pull a lot off. He starts as a very optimistic, fun, playful, young guy in love, and in this movie has to turn into somebody that’s much closer to the Haymitch that we’re used to—cynical and a drunk. He’s going to have to go through a lot of emotional trauma, plus have that kind of mischievousness, irreverence, all these different elements that Woody [Harrelson] has naturally. And so we really put him through the ringer. We did a lot of tests, kept bringing him back, bringing him back, bringing him back. He and I were modulating how much Woody we feel in his performance.

I want to make sure that everybody makes the role their own. That they find the spirit of the character and that it’s not trying to do an imitation of somebody. That’s true of Elle [Fanning] doing Effie, of Ralph [Fiennes] doing Snow, of Jesse [Plemons] doing Plutarch, Kieran [Culkin] as Caesar. Everybody has to figure out how to do it on their own. Then the weird thing is that Kelvin [Harrison Jr., who plays a young Beetee], has worked with Jeffrey [Wright] three times. So he’s fairly close with Jeffrey. When he got the role, he called and said, “You won’t believe this, but I’m actually playing the young version of you.” He could just conjure Jeffrey Wright. His voice, the speech patterns, the timbre of the sound of everything. It was pretty wild.

Were there storylines from the previous films that you felt you could plant Easter eggs for? I’m thinking specifically of the romantic chemistry between Effie and Haymitch.

There are certain Capitol characters where I give a lot of freedom for improvisation. Effie, Caesar, Drusilla [played by Glenn Close], there’s a lot of room for ad-libs. One of the elements that we definitely played with a bit came from an improvised moment in the [last] Mockingjay. We were shooting this scene in Atlanta outside of Snow’s mansion, which is one of the very last scenes of Katniss in the Capitol. She’s saying goodbye to Effie, and then Haymitch and Effie kiss.

Quite honestly, it was an idea because Woody just wanted to kiss Elizabeth Banks. But everybody thought it would be fun and that the fans would dig it, that Haymitch kissed her. Then it became this big thing of this hidden love that Haymitch and Effie have for one another. And Elle played into that a bit. So there’s, I would say, a hint of flirtation here between the two, less so on Haymitch’s side. His heart is obviously somewhere else in the story. But Elle definitely brought a bit of that to it. That was not scripted. That’s the fun of having great actors.

What was it like to reunite Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson from the original movies?

Jen and I have stayed close over the years. We’ve done four movies together. Josh, who basically has moved to Spain, I haven’t seen in a long time. Woody I see off and on and text every once in a while. But there was something really special about the three of them being back together.

It’s also really, for the most part, the same crew from 2012, when we started making Catching Fire. It’s the same DP [Jo Willems], the same camera operator [David J. Thompson], the same AD [Christopher Surgent].

[When] they got to the hotel, Jen and Josh were in the bar having a beer or something, and I was like, Okay, I won’t even shower. I won’t get out of my rain gear. I’ll just come in. The next thing you know, there were 40 of us who had been together since Catching Fire, the gang back together. It’s like a high school reunion or something, but in the best possible way.

There’s a futility to what happens in this film, knowing where we end up in future movies. How do you handle that aspect of history being doomed to repeat itself?

Look, we’re doing a story where you know the lead character is going to make it out. It’s really about how he makes it out, and what he ends up being like at the end of it all. What I’m really pleased about is that the way Suzanne wrote the book, and the way I think we’ve ended the movie, there is a sense of hope that the tragedy is not for nothing. That was really important to me. And one of the beautiful elements in the story, which comes a bit later, is this sense of, everybody has to find their voice. Everybody has to participate.

It really deals with this thing that I think is happening a lot today, where you find apathy: people not wanting to vote, feeling even if they do vote that it’s not going to matter. This idea that you have to be active, and you can’t expect immediate gratification—that everybody needs to stand up and it may take generations, but you still have to do it.

Outside of my screening on the Upper West Side, there was a group protesting Elon Musk and data centers because the documentary about him was playing at the theater. It was a reminder that there will always be something to rise up against, and always people who will be willing to do it.

Yeah, exactly. And ideally, at some point, if everybody stands up, something will change.

During the 13 years that you’ve worked in this universe, dystopia has felt more and more familiar. How have real-world events influenced your filmmaking?

In the 56 years I’ve been alive, there’s never really been a time where I’ve felt like, Oh wow, everything is great. Nothing is wrong in the world. It always feels like there’s some dystopian sense about the world at any given time. And somehow Suzanne is always able to write these stories about it, which is what makes these movies feel timeless. A lot of people just see them as spectacles, but really they’re about our times very specifically. Almost in a subversive way, I feel like we’ve gotten to smuggle these ideas into these movies that a lot of people go see.

#3507. Would Lindsay Arnold Ever Return as 'DWTS' Pro? What She's Said

Lindsay Arnold has taken some time away from the Dancing With the Stars ballroom, but would she ever return?

Arnold made her debut as a DWTS pro for season 16 in 2013, one year after competing on season 9 of So You Think You Can Dance. At the time, Arnold was the second-youngest pro in DWTS history.

Following her first season, Arnold performed with the troupe for seasons 17 through 20. She was bumped up to pro status once again for season 21 in 2015, landing in third place with partner Alek Skarlatos.

Arnold competed as a pro for 10 seasons before announcing in 2022 that she wouldn’t be returning.

“This has been one of the hardest decisions to make, but ultimately, I have chosen what I feel is best for myself and my family,” the choreographer — who shares three children with husband Sam Cusick — wrote via Instagram at the time, adding that she still loved the show “with all of my heart.”

Since then, Arnold has frequently been asked whether she’d ever perform in the DWTS ballroom again. (Fans will see her make a cameo in sister Rylee Arnold‘s freestyle with Connor Wood during the season 35 finale.)

Scroll down for everything to know about whether Lindsay will return as a DWTS pro:

From her 10 seasons as a pro, Lindsay has one mirrorball trophy. She won season 25 in 2017 with actor Jordan Fisher. Lindsay and MLB alum David Ross were runners-up on season 24. She landed in third place with Skarlatos on season 21 and with Calvin Johnson Jr. on season 23.

Lindsay last competed on DWTS with former Bachelor Matt James on season 30 in 2021, ending in 12th place — the lowest ranking in her career.

While speaking with Us in 2024, Lindsay said she “would love” to return to DWTS in some capacity. “[I] definitely have already expressed [that] I’d love to be there if it ever makes sense or needs to happen, or whatever,” she explained.

At the time, Lindsay added that it was “really fun” to support her sister Rylee, who joined the show as a pro in 2023.

“Genuinely I feel like I’m in it with Rylee because I’m like, ‘Send me every video, call me after rehearsal, tell me everything.’ I feel like I’m so in it,” Lindsay said. “It’s funny, because I feel like I even get a little bit more stressed and worried and into it than I ever did for myself because it’s my little baby sister.”

Ahead of season 35, Lindsay told Us she would “never say never” to competing again. “There’s so many aspects of it that I miss,” she said. “In a perfect world, I could do the show and also do all the other things I have and also take my kids to all of their things and also be home. … But I think right now, I am just absolutely loving and embracing this phase of life that we’re in.”

Throughout her own DWTS journey, Rylee has been candid about how much Lindsay has shown her support.

In 2024, Rylee told Us she tried “so hard” to get her older sister back on the show, teasing, “I think there is probably a future with Dancing With the Stars and Lindsay.”

Rylee later revealed Lindsay is “always there” to give her positive feedback. “I call her all the time in rehearsals, and I’m like, ‘Do you like this dance move? Is this good?'” she said amid season 35. “So, she’s a part of this whole process for me, and she’s the best.”

Dancing With The Stars Season 35 finale is here, and it's always bittersweet for the competitors. Losing can be a bummer, but not as painful as it is for some of these celebrities to say goodbye to the pros they've been working with every day for the past couple of months. Tatyana Ali is going to miss Jan Ravnik, and her touching words to him have me in my feels.

Ali shared her goodbye message to Jan on Instagram ahead of the finale's premiere on the 2026 TV schedule, presumably so they can lock in on finale night and wow the judges with their last dances. If it wasn't clear throughout the season, Tatyana confirmed she loved working with her dance partner:

As I’ve said before, meeting you and getting to know you has been the best part of this whole thing. I am going to miss seeing you every day. I’m going to miss singing with you. I’m going to miss laughing with you. You are one of the most exceptional people I have ever met in my life.

The duo is in the midst of a Cinderella run, in which the fan vote helped propel them to the semifinals and the finale after Jenna Dewan and Harry Shum Jr. were voted out instead. She's now in a position to be a Mirrorball winner who had the lowest Week 1 score of all time, assuming she can get the votes over some other fan favorites.

It's a credit not just to her improvement as a dancer, but to Jan Ravnik, who came under fire from former pros last season. Maks Chmerkovskiy took shots at Ravnik for not being a professionally trained ballroom dancer, and said he was unworthy of being a performer on the show. This finale appearance disproved that, and if Ravnik needed any more reminders of that, Tatyana Ali had more words of encouragement:

Your drive, your hard work, your passion, and your brilliance are astounding. You inspire me. You’re my friend. For life. I just adore you.  And there’s nothing I could say in this video that I that you don’t actually know. You have a light that is so bright, and everything you’ve got: The way you carry yourself, the way you handle situations, exactly as it should be. Don’t ever accept any less than you deserve because you deserve it all. You’re a star. In the realest. The realest, most soulful version of that word. I love you.

It's been a long road for both of them, and they've had doubters along the way who questioned whether they'd rise to the occasion. I would reckon those doubters are gone ahead of the finale and ready to see what they have planned for the big night.

The duo are planning to perform a salsa to “Jamaican (Bam Bam)” by HUGEL & SOLTO, a freestyle dance set to Cab Calloway's "Minnie the Moocher," and will close with Judy Garland's "Somewhere Over the Rainbow." That's quite a lineup, and I'm especially excited to see how she and Jan tackle Calloway's classic tune.

Win or lose, Jan and Tatyana's journey has potentially changed the dancing series forever. Sharna Burgess and others are up in arms about the voting situation and wondering if fans have too much power in dictating who should and shouldn't be in the finals. I'll be interested to see how this conversation evolves in the off-season, and if changes are on the way for fan voting.

Dancing With The Stars finale kicks off on ABC on Tuesday, November 24th on ABC or for those with a Disney+ subscription at 8:00 p.m. ET. I'm sure the conversation will go much further than finale night, so stick around to see what all gets said.

#3505. GTA 6 Has A Super Mario Bros. Easter Egg, And It’s A Trip

Grand Theft Auto 6 has plenty of fun Easter eggs--many of which tie back to earlier games in the series--but you can also find a few nods to other megapopular game franchises hiding within the vast map of Leonida. If you take a detour along the north side of Lummox County, you'll come across an area in the woods that looks like it'd be right at home in a Super Mario Bros. game, and you can even collect two distinct caps for your troubles--which might suggest that the greater Mario multiverse theory is true after all.

How to find the GTA 6 Super Mario Bros. Easter egg in GTA 6

You can mark this location on your map, as you can find the reference to the Nintendo mascot in Lummox County. It's up north from Mount Kalaga, at the end of a twisty road that seemingly goes nowhere:

Hit the bong, dude

Once you've arrived, scout the area for a purple tarp that has a bong sitting on it. Smoke it, get high, and climb the structure in front of you. You'll notice that there's a plume of smoke coming out of the one column, and if you stand in it, an invisible block will appear above your head.

Smash the block

Jump up, and you'll smash the block. You won't get any gold coins for your trouble, but you will get a nostalgic tune and two caps that reference Nintendo's favorite plumbers, Mario and Luigi.

Collect the caps

Each cap has an initial embroidered on it: "J" for Jason, "L" for Lucia. You can add them to your collection, or leave them to gather dust; it's up to you. 

As mentioned above, GTA 6 has references to a lot of pop culture. Someone at Rockstar Games is clearly a huge Dexter fan, Bigfoot is on the prowl, and I really wish I'd chosen the elevator without a killer clown inside it. For everything else on the biggest game of the year--and maybe even the decade--check out GameSpot's GTA 6 guides hub.

#3504. Capcom’s Live-Service Dino Shooter Is Going Offline Forever Just Four Years Later

Capcom’s live-service dino shooter Exoprimal officially has an end date. Servers will go offline for good in September 2027, just a little over four years after it originally launched day-and-date with Game Pass. You can still buy it for $60, for some reason.

“We regret to announce that service for Exoprimal will be discontinued as of 8:00 PM (PDT) on Wednesday, September 29, 2027,” the Resident Evil publisher announced this week. “We cannot thank you enough for the love and support you have shown over the years, and we sincerely apologize for the gravity of this announcement.”

The end of service won’t come as a shock to anyone who’s been following the game’s trajectory. Launched in July 2023, it was an early-comer to the wave of post-covid online multiplayer games that have all quickly been abandoned in the years since. Capcom pulled the plug on additional content updates just 12 months into the game’s life.

Premium passes and microtransactions were still being sold, however. That all ended this week on November 24 alongside the end of service announcement. The game itself and all its DLC will be delisted from consoles and PC on March 30, 2027. Those who already purchased the game will still be able to re-download it and play until the servers go offline.

That is unlikely to be many people. The shooter peaked at eight concurrent players on Steam today. While the shooter had a unique sensibility and some cool horde mechanics, it wasn’t the spiritual Dino Crisis revival most fans had hoped for. Instead, it ended up another example of the industry’s wasted efforts to cash in on the latest gaming fad, and further proof of all the things the Stop Killing Games crowd has been warning people about.

#3503. GTA 6: All The Secret Controls And Gameplay Features You Might Have Missed

On the surface, Grand Theft Auto 6 has a pretty standard control scheme for its protagonists. You've got everything you'd expect for exploring its open-world environment, from options to sprint to aiming your gun, but there's a whole lot more to the game when you start experimenting with the inputs. Whether you're driving or jogging, Jason and Lucia are capable of a whole lot more, and these hidden features aren't thrown at you when you start the game.

Instead, you're left to discover them as you play, and each one adds another layer of immersion to the experience. If you don't want to accidentally stumble on them, here's a closer look at every hidden gameplay feature we've discovered so far. For more on GTA 6, from completing side missions to finding a tricky location on the sprawling map of Leonida, we’ve got you covered with our Grand Theft Auto 6 guides hub.

Go into first-person mode

Want to examine the world in more detail around you? Press L2 (LT on Xbox) to highlight something, then press R3 to go into first-person mode. Ordinarily, you can't move around in this mode, but there is a glitch to force the game to lock you into first-person.

Change shoulder cameras

Not too big a fan of the default over-the-shoulder aiming in GTA 6? You can switch which shoulder you aim from during combat by holding the left button on your D-pad while aiming with L2.

Quick-swap between weapons

At the same time, you can also quick-swap between weapons by tapping Triangle/Y while aiming, allowing you to keep blastin' like you're some sort of Frank Reynolds character.

Do a combat roll!

Need to close the gap quickly and avoid taking a few lead injections? Tap X/A while aiming, and you'll do a combat roll.

Do a backflip!

To show off some athleticism, run towards water, and as you get to the edge, hold X/A on the controller to do a backflip.

Pistol-whip when you're out of bullets

Got a gun in your hand, but you're out of bullets? It turns out that firearms are still good for inflicting blunt-force trauma, as you can use the melee attack (Square on PS5, X on Xbox) to knock enemies out.

Choke enemies out

For a stealthy beatdown, start a fight in GTA 6, grapple your opponent with R2, and then hold Square/X to set them up for a chokehold. Press the indicated D-pad button on your controller, and you'll trigger the chokehold.

Chain-jump across gaps

If you're running across an area that has multiple small gaps, you can tap X to jump across and tap it again to keep your momentum going.

Your car door is also a weapon

Instead of damaging the hood of your car in GTA 6, put a dent in your door by smashing it into a pedestrian. Like melee attacks, you can hit Square/X on your controller while driving to nail an unlucky person with the door.

Your feet are technically free when you're on a bike

And if you're not in a car? You can relive your Road Rash days by hitting the melee button to kick someone instead while you scoot around on a bike.

Change how you wear your cap

Whether you like to wear your cap in a traditional sun-blocking style or backwards, you can swap the position of your headwear easily. Just open the items and weapon wheel by holding L1, select items, and navigate to your cap. Press X/A and you can switch styles.

Distract enemies with some whistling, which I can't do in real life

GTA 6 makes for a surprisingly good stealth game, and for those scenarios where you need to draw enemy attention, you can whistle at them. Crouch, take cover, hold L2 to aim at a target, and press Triangle/Y to whistle.

Loiter like a champ with leaning actions

One of the cooler features in GTA 6 for photography fans is the option to lean against walls and railings. When you're near a wall, you can hold Circle/B to lean against it, and when next to a railing, press L3 to rest on that structure--pretty cool for when you want to take a photograph of Jason or Lucia while they chill out. If you're on solid ground, you can also hold down Circle/B to sit down.

Choose your favorite hand

If you want Jason or Lucia to emulate your dominant hand while they're holding something, press left or right on the D-pad. You can also make them hold two items at the same time, in case you want to show off that you're one of the lucky even-handed few.

Auto-drive to destinations 

One of our favorite modes in the game--especially when we want to soak in the scenery of Vice City--auto-drive is pretty easy to miss. While you're driving, hold the down button on the D-pad, press Start to enable Cinematic Mode, and then hold Circle/B to switch to auto-drive mode. You can also set the speed between slow/normal/fast for your commute.

Quick-scan vehicles

Instead of navigating to your WAiNK app, just hold Up on your D-Pad to bring it up instantly.

Duck while driving so you can avoid being shot

You're going to be in plenty of high-speed shootouts in GTA 6, and if you want to keep your head on your shoulders, hold the Circle/B button while driving to duck down.

You have turn signals; use them

Unless you're driving the equivalent of a BMW in GTA 6, you should use turn signals. While you're in your car, tap left or right on your D-pad to use these lights. They'll also cancel automatically after you've made a turn.

Switch car headlights on and off

Want to drive in stealth mode at night? Tap the circle button to turn off your headlights. Just don't be too surprised if other motorists flash you with their lights to remind you that you're driving dark.

Leave the engine running

Want to prepare your vehicle to be in getaway mode for a heist that you're about to pull off? You can leave the engine running by double-tapping Triangle/Y as you exit your car. Just be aware that this could invite car thieves to swipe your vehicle, since you're leaving it out there and purring. If you do this while piloting a boat, it'll also sail on while you explore the deck.

Push vehicles

In case you're stuck in a ditch or out of fuel, you can push your vehicle to safety. Position yourself behind, next to, or in front of your car (or boat), and keep pushing your character into it with the left stick until they switch to a pushing animation. Hold Square/X to move the vehicle, or flip it in case it has been overturned or beached.

Leave your car door open

You can also shave valuable seconds off your getaway by keeping your car door open. As you exit your car, press triangle once.

Slide across your car hood

For some Dukes of Hazzard action, sprint towards your car, aim for the hood, and tap X to slide across it. Yeehaw.

Drop anchor

If you don't want your boat to sail away without you while you search the ocean depths for treasure, make certain that you drop anchor. Press and hold left on the D-pad while piloting a boat, navigate to the vehicle menu with the right analog stick, and choose Anchor to lower it.

Additional vehicle controls

On that note, you can also find extra vehicle controls by bringing up the radio menu (press and hold left on the D-pad), and using the right analogue stick to navigate up.

Turn radios on and off instantly

If you're anything like me and your ears start to bleed when you boost a car that has the country music station turned on, double-tap left on the D-pad to instantly switch it off.

You can smoke while driving

Not that you should because it's bad for your health and both hands should be on the steering wheel, but you can hold L1 to bring up your items wheel, select cigarettes or a cigar, and then select R1 or R2 to start puffing away.

Flick a cigarette

You can also flick your cigarette when you're done smoking by holding the R2 button. Aim, and do that after you've poured out a trail of fuel on the ground, for extra cinema-style points.

Flip the bird while driving

The universal hand sign for telling someone that their driving is not up to par can easily be done by aiming at a motorist with L2 and then pressing R1 on your controller.

Trash talk drivers

Or if you need to give some verbal abuse, pull up next to another driver, press L2 to aim at them, and press R3 to give them some grief. Just don't be too surprised if they respond violently to your provocations.
