#3374. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

#3373. 7 Funniest MST3K Episodes to Watch For Your Personal Turkey Day Marathon

We gather together to watch cheesy movies

Mystery Science Theater 3000 fans have always had a special relationship with American Thanksgiving. The show originally premiered on Thanksgiving Day in 1988, back in its public access era on KTMA TV in Minneapolis. Three years later, Comedy Central ran the first "Turkey Day" MST3K marathon, as both an anniversary celebration for the show and a 30-hour Thanksgiving special.

The Turkey Day tradition got dropped when MST3K moved from Comedy Central to the Sci-Fi Channel in 1997. (While Sci-Fi did run a MST3K marathon on Thanksgiving 1997, it wasn't labeled "Turkey Day.") That was the end of the tradition until 2013, when MST3K’s DVD distributor Shout! Factory revived Turkey Day via livestream.

2026's Turkey Day celebration, Back in Orbit, features six episodes from the Sci-Fi Channel run, as introduced by Mike Nelson, Kevin Murphy, and Bill Corbett. This is both a nod to their time as the hosts of the show during its Sci-Fi Channel run and a tie-in to the recently concluded MST3K/Rifftrax crossover spinoff, The Rifftrax Experiments.

This year's Turkey Day starts on Nov. 26 at noon EST on the official MST3K YouTube and Twitch channels, and is currently scheduled to feature:

That's a solid lineup of late-season MST3K. However, if you're interested in alternative programming (or you simply want a marathon on a day other than American Thanksgiving this year), just about all of the first 10 seasons of MST3K can be found for free on YouTube, either from old fan uploads or via the official MST3K channel. Due to MST3K's famous "keep circulating the tapes" mantra, the old uploads are the next best thing to officially endorsed, so you can binge guilt-free. Here are some more MST3K episodes to consider for your own Thanksgiving entertainment, sorted by their original broadcast order.

“I’m the luckiest boy in the world! I have slipped the surly bonds of Earth and touched the hand of God!”

MST3K really hit its stride in season 3. There are a few good episodes in the first two seasons, such as Catalina Caper and Robot Monster, but season 3 features a stacked roster of series-defining classics, and it starts with this hastily-made Italian fantasy film.

Cave Dwellers is a rebrand of the second movie in a four-part franchise starring the fantasy hero Ator (Miles O'Keefe). There's this whole rich vein of cheap B-movie sword-and-sorcery films from the mid-to-late 1980s that were all trying to cash in on the success of Arnold Schwarzenegger's Conan the Barbarian, and most of them are Italian knock-offs that were made in a week. The best of them are dumb fun; the worst are cocaine-infused unwatchable dreck.

What sets Cave Dwellers apart from the pack is that it takes some really big swings. It feels like one big continuity error even before the climactic moment where Ator instantly and inexplicably invents both hand grenades and the hang glider. It's a nearly perfect bad movie, both in its own right and as fodder for an MST3K episode.

“Hey, what gives? I’m on the milk carton.”

This was the episode that made MST3K click for me. Any B-movie fan knows there's a world of difference between "fun bad" and simply bad, and Pod People is about as fun-bad as it gets.

The backstory is reportedly that Spanish director Juan Piquer Simón (Pieces) set out to make a straightforward horror movie about a vacationing pop band that stumbles across a murderous alien. Then E.T. got popular, so Simón's producers demanded a reshoot to include an additional subplot about a boy who befriends an alien child.

The result was released in France and Spain as 1983's Extra Terrestrial Visitors, before being retitled to The Unearthling and Pod People for overseas release. It's a baffling mixture of at least three major plotlines, stitched together with little care for the final product. One moment is a heartwarming story of a child and his plush marketable alien pal; the next is some dude in a fursuit killing his way through a set of backup singers. That tonal mismatch makes Pod People a nearly perfect target for MST3K, which led to several of the show's most famous jokes.

“Every frame of this movie looks like someone’s last known photograph.”

To no one's real surprise, Manos is still generally considered the best episode of MST3K's run on Comedy Central, if not the single best episode. There are other good episodes in the fourth season, like City Limits and Hercules Unchained, but Manos overshadows them all. Like Pod People, this episode dug a notorious dud out of the back alleys of cinematic history and turned it most of the way into comedy gold.

I only say "most of the way" because Manos is a rough watch, even with Joel and the bots running interference. It's a truly baffling independent horror film from 1966, made with faulty equipment on a shoestring budget by a fertilizer salesman who allegedly did it all to win a bet. Manos is just so damn weird that it’s difficult to sit through. It was only ever screened at a handful of theaters in Texas before it appeared on MST3K, at which point it instantly became a legend.

Every frame of Manos is simply uncomfortable. The cast and crew of MST3K were always quite clear in behind-the-scenes featurettes that by the time they sat down to film an episode of the show, they'd watched the entirety of that episode’s featured movie at least five times. Despite that, Joel and the bots still manage to come off as realistically flabbergasted by each bizarre twist in Manos. There's a distinct point at which it stops being a classic MST3K episode and becomes pure trainwreck syndrome, whether you’ve seen the movie before or not.

Much like how Cave Dwellers is a reaction to the success of Conan the Barbarian, Escape 2000 (originally released as Escape From the Bronx, and not to be confused with the 1982 Australian humans-hunting-humans film) is an Italian clone of the first two Mad Max movies. It's set in a dystopian near-future New York City, as the gangs of the Bronx team up to defend their borough from a mega-corporation that wants to destroy and rebuild it. Come to think of it, Escape 2000 predicted gentrification.

Escape 2000 isn't actually that bad of a film. It's just cheaply made, overwrought, and has the same low-quality English dub as a lot of other '80s Italian B-movies, so if you’ve got a taste for that sort of thing you can have a good time with it. That makes it a solid target for the MST3K crew, which instantly lock in on a half-dozen running jokes in the first 10 minutes. It's hard to hear the word "Bronx" after this episode and not immediately think, "None of this would have happened if they'd just left the Bronx."

The first 10 seasons of MST3K were filmed in Minnesota, which neatly explains why the show was always so comfortable poking fun at Canadians. With that in mind, The Final Sacrifice is one long joke at Canada's expense, even before Mike and the bots sit down.

In another example of MST3K pulling a movie out of obscurity, 1990's The Final Sacrifice was made by a film student in Alberta on a budget of CA$1,500. Apparently it aired a few times on Canadian television in the early '90s, but was virtually unknown outside the country until its MST3K appearance.

The saving grace of The Final Sacrifice, both as a film and as an MST3K episode, is Zap Rowsdower (Bruce J. Mitchell). He might have the dumbest name of any character in film history, he's the sidekick until he's suddenly the hero in the last act, and he's a big buttery beer-fed ball of Canadian stereotypes. In other words, he's perfect. No notes. In a more perfect universe than this, Rowsdower would be on his tenth major motion picture, as he fights and drinks his way through unexplored Canadian action history. It's easily the highlight of this year's Turkey Day celebration, as it was hard to find online until recently, and it's worth incorporating into your own custom marathon.

”Why is he so impossible to hit? How can they keep missing this slow, giant white thing?”

Space Mutiny is still perhaps the most quotable episode of MST3K, even 29 years after it aired. It's given the internet decades of running jokes and forum handles, all at the expense of famous chunkhead Blast Hardcheese Punch Rockgroin Dave Ryder (Reb Brown, Yor, the Hunter From the Future) and his battle to save a colony ship from mutineers.

The co-stars of Space Mutiny have insisted since its release that it was meant to be a campy spoof of science fiction, but that's obviously damage control. Instead, it's obviously a million-dollar script paired with a buck-fifty budget. At its best, Space Mutiny is funny for all the wrong reasons, from Reb Brown’s random screaming to every woman on the colony ship wearing exercise gear as a “uniform” to the space battles that consist of visibly recycled footage from the original Battlestar Galactica. Its MST3K episode is one of the best in the series' run, often held up as the best in the Sci-Fi Channel seasons, and a genuine classic.

“You asked for an avalanche of flavor, and now you got it, huh? Not enjoying it, are you?”

While MST3K has always been known for its high volume of jokes, the Netflix seasons have a particular rushed delivery that can work against them. There are still a few great episodes in the two-season run, however, and Avalanche is a dark horse contender for the best of the lot.

Avalanche is a 1978 disaster movie produced by schlock auteur Roger Corman, starring Rock Hudson and Mia Farrow, who have less than zero chemistry with one another. They play a divorced couple, and it's obvious within seconds of seeing them together that there were multiple good reasons for that divorce.

That isn't Avalanche's biggest problem, however. In the best low-budget tradition, it saves all its special effects for the finale, which makes it a disaster movie where the titular disaster doesn't show up until the last 20 minutes. That leaves the viewer to sit through an hour of awkward foreshadowing, personal dramas, and horrible '70s dinner parties (there's a baked Alaska in Avalanche that's so unappetizing that it deserves its own unique content warning) until half the cast gets murdered by snow. The MST3K crew makes the best of it with some of the best jokes in season 11. It's an unsung hero of Jonah Ray's time as MST3K's host.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3372. Why Rachel McAdams Turned Down The Role Of Pepper Potts In Marvel's Iron Man

As Tony Stark's (Robert Downey Jr.) girl Friday and eventual wife Pepper Potts, Gwyneth Paltrow is one of the longest lasting Marvel Cinematic Universe actors. She portrayed Pepper throughout the very first MCU film, 2008's "Iron Man," and was last seen in 2019's "Avengers: Endgame." Then again, it's also a meme that Paltrow barely remembers details of the Marvel movies she was in, down to forgetting altogether how she appeared in "Spider-Man: Homecoming."

Paltrow was not the "Iron Man" team's original first choice for Pepper. In December 2006, Umberto Gonzalez of Latino Review reported that Marvel Studios sent the "Iron Man" script exclusively to Rachel McAdams, hoping to cast her as Pepper. McAdams was riding a rising tide, having broken out in 2004 by playing Regina George in "Mean Girls" and Allie Hamilton in "The Notebook." The following year, she also starred in Wes Craven's hit airplane thriller "Red Eye." It makes sense that Marvel would've want to hire her, especially with "Iron Man" not being a guaranteed hit back then, but she declined. That, of course, opened the door for Paltrow's casting.

Speaking to Bustle in 2023, McAdams noted "Iron Man" was just one of several blockbusters she turned down in that time period, including "Casino Royale," "Mission: Impossible III," and "The Devil Wears Prada." Why? Simple, she'd been swept up off her feet into movie stardom and wanted to readjust with time for herself. Looking at McAdams' filmography, you'll notice she was largely on an acting break between 2006 and 2008 — she appeared in only two films (2007's "Married Life" and 2008's "The Lucky Ones") in that stretch.

"I knew I was in such a lucky spot, but I also knew it wasn't quite jiving with my personality and what I needed to stay sane," McAdams told Bustle.

Rachel McAdams' decision to take a break hardly killed her Hollywood momentum. To this day, McAdams enjoys a very healthy acting career, with her accolades including a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nomination for "Spotlight." Amusingly, the first blockbuster she accepted a part in after her semi-hiatus was the 2009 "Sherlock Holmes" movie, directed by Guy Ritchie and starring... Robert Downey Jr., who'd just had his leading man status bolstered higher than ever by "Iron Man."

McAdams stars in "Sherlock Holmes" as the thief Irene Adler, Holmes' love interest. Now, Irene is more Catwoman (arguably the original Catwoman) than Pepper Potts, but "Sherlock Holmes" still shows McAdams and RDJ had chemistry aplenty. It's the closest we can get to tangible proof that, had she played Pepper, "Iron Man" (and the Marvel movies that followed) would've turned out just fine.

Marvel Studios didn't forget McAdams' number, either, considering she eventually starred in "Doctor Strange" as Dr. Christine Palmer, Stephen Strange's (Benedict Cumberbatch) ex. (Literally casting the woman who turned down Pepper Potts definitely makes "Doctor Strange" feel even more like wizard "Iron Man" than it already does.) McAdams later returned for the sequel, "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," which introduced her to director Sam Raimi.

Raimi, believing "Doctor Strange" wasn't the best showcase for McAdams, promised himself to work with her again. He thus cast McAdams in his subsequent movie, the survival thriller comedy "Send Help," featuring McAdams as an overlooked office drone who gets stuck on a desert island with her a-hole boss (Dylan O'Brien). "Send Help" features McAdams' most delightfully twisted performance yet — but if she'd agreed to "Iron Man" all those years ago, it's quite possible the dominos of her career would've fallen differently.

#3371. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3370. Oobah Butler Wants to Expose the World’s Stupidest Industries, but They Get Worse Faster Than He Can Plan His Stunts

It’s a spectacular time to be a grifter. Basic truths keep getting harder for people to agree on, marketing is more dependent on hackable algorithms than traditional gatekeepers, and it seems like everyone is willing to uncritically listen to anyone offering them a shortcut. As Oobah Butler puts it in the first episode of his new HBO series “Scams for a Better Tomorrow,” we’re living through a “gold rush of bullshit.”

If that’s the case, Butler is a prospector who hits a paystreak everywhere he looks. After beginning his career as a musician, the British performance artist has devoted much of his past decade to the art of the scam. In 2017, he made headlines for creating a TripAdvisor profile for a nonexistent restaurant that briefly became the highest-rated eatery in London. His penchant for scams has only grown since then, culminating in “Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow.” The five-episode, “Nathan for You”-esque series sees him grift his way to the top of some of the slimiest industries on the planet including wellness supplements, wine, and dating apps with an approach that blurs the line between satire and how-to guides. Related Stories Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

When we spoke over Zoom, it was the first time I had ever interviewed a scammer. I naturally had to ask Butler if that was his preferred term (he had no problem with it), and how he would characterize his own unorthodox line of work.

“I think it sits somewhere between gonzo journalism and comedy. And I think we’re in a moment, in a culture, that’s just so rife with inauthenticity and scamming,” Butler said, explaining that just watching run-of-the-mill advertisements on a streaming service are enough to convince you that we live in an insane world. “One in three [ads] are AI now. And I don’t know why, that stuck in my mind recently where I was like, ‘Wow, these aren’t real people trying to sell me a product. They’re like prompts in a machine.’ So it’s an interesting line of work, but I think it feels very now, to be honest.”

The series should be essential viewing for anyone who either wants to laugh at the state of our seemingly elite spaces or just wants to make a quick buck in a dirty industry. Episodes illustrate how ecosystems of influencers and online ratings can be easily manipulated in pursuit of accomplishing ludicrous goals, like turning an undrinkable bottle of smoke tainted cabernet into one of Napa’s highest-rated wines of the year or marketing a skincare product as “endorsed by Cameron Diaz” because a random Hispanic guy was willing to slap his name on it for $50.

It’s a funny enough premise, but Oobah and his small team (which included frequent Safdie collaborator Ronald Bronstein) found that their best laid plans left them insufficiently prepared for the greed and stupidity that they’d encounter in the real world. The first episode begins with a scheme to market a new skin serum that’s allegedly made from the tears of small children. They thought that ridiculous idea could serve as the climax of an episode, but they soon found that the grifters they encountered had little issue with the idea — some of them even thought they could make money on it with the right tear-shaped bottle. The joke remained in the show, but it had to be reduced to a starting point before the episode devolved into crazier plans.

“We had a tip from a journalist that dermatologists can be full of shit and that they often can take money in exchange for recommendations. So we set up a lab where I had these kid actors with goggles on with tubes coming off them, and it was like we were milking the kids for the tears or whatever. We were like, ‘Right, we’re going to invite this dermatologist down here,’ a high-end Manhattan dermatologist, and we expected the dermatologist to laugh us out of the room,” he said. “What we couldn’t plan for doing that stunt is that the dermatologist would be like, ‘Awesome. Yeah, this is cool. Yeah, all right, interesting product. Maybe we could keep on working together, but I expect an endorsement fee.’ And I’m like, ‘Oh, you don’t give a fucking shit. You don’t care.'”

The incident cuts to the central problem of a show like this: it’s hard for satire to keep up with a world that only seems to get crazier every day. But Butler is not shying away from the challenge. He works quickly (the show began shooting this spring and wrapped in October before premiering on November 22), and is willing to change his plans whenever it turns out that a sincere actor has beaten him to one of his comedic scams. He already has plenty of ideas for a hypothetical Season 2, including taking on the recent trend of hotels and vacation rentals using AI-generated images that look nothing like their actual rooms. But the one thing he can count on is that the bullshit gold rush is not going to end any time soon.

“It’s hard to satirize something that’s so insane and fucked up,” he said. “That’s why in the first episode, we go and make a new product because it felt like the children’s tears thing wasn’t crazy enough. You know what I mean? So I literally go and make a human meat supplement, a lab-grown human meat supplement, and we go to this lab in Austin, we take stem cells from my stomach, we grow it over months and we create this thing. Because the actual reason we did that was like, ‘Oh, I don’t think children’s tears is scary because influencers would promote that.’ So I suppose that the crazier things get, the crazier the satire has to be able for it to be effective.”

“Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow” airs Sunday nights on HBO at 11 p.m. ET/PT before streaming on HBO Max.

#3369. 12 Most Devastating Deaths In The Hunger Games Movies, Ranked

Warning! This post contains SPOILERS for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the ReapingThe Hunger Games movies have some of the most devastating deaths in all of cinema. This includes the newly released Sunrise on The Reaping, which details Panem's second Quarter Quell and Haymitch's victory nearly 25 years before the events of the first Hunger Games movie with Katniss Everdeen.

Whether it's countless children being forced to fight to the death and/or those who choose to resist the Capitol, the Hunger Games franchise has delivered several truly heartbreaking moments. While this can come from the loss of characters who'd been developed over the course of several movies, even those with minimal screen time can still meet fates that are incredibly hard to watch.

When trying to determine the most tragic fate in the franchise, the list below considers the circumstances of each character's death, the emotional impact, and what the loss means for the franchise narrative at large. Keeping that in mind, here's our ranking of the 12 most heartbreaking deaths across all The Hunger Games movies and prequels, including Sunrise on the Reaping.

Wyatt Callow's death is one of the earliest tragedies in Sunrise on the Reaping once the 50th Hunger Games actually begin.

One of the four tributes chosen from District 12, Wyatt rushes to protect the younger Lou Lou and is quickly killed with an axe to the back from Silka, one of the vicious career tributes. This happened mere moments after the very start of the Games. While it may not be the most gruesome death in the franchise, it's truly heartbreaking to see Wyatt die so suddenly after all the time spent in the first act of the movie introducing him along with his fellow District 12 tributes.

Having been an Oddsmaker back in District 12, there's a cruel irony that the odds clearly weren't in Wyatt's favor the moment he himself was put into the Hunger Games.

The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes' Wovey is one of the youngest tributes in the 10th Hunger Games, making her death particularly hard to watch.

Representing District 8, Wovey held Lucy Gray's hand as they walked into the arena and hid for almost all of the games. She only came out when she heard the large Capitol drone overhead, thinking the Games were over. Instead, she was one of the first to be completely overwhelmed by the horde of venomous and genetically altered rainbow-colored snakes dropped into the arena. Having stood very little chance of actually surviving the Games beyond her ability to climb and hide, Wovey's death is easily one of the most heartbreaking in Songbirds and Snakes.

In the main Hunger Games series, Cinna is one of Katniss' most important allies. A fashion designer secretly supporting the ongoing rebellion against the Capitol, Cinna's designs for Katniss became symbols of resistance, culminating with the transformation of her wedding dress into a Mockingjay in Catching Fire, a moment that cemented Katniss as the ultimate symbol of rebellion.

As a result, Cinna is arrested and beaten by Capitol Peacekeepers just before she enters the arena for the third Quarter Quell. It wasn't until after Katniss was extracted by the rebellion and taken to District 13 that she would learn of Cinna's tragic off-screen death during interrogation. Nevertheless, seeing him beaten and dragged away toward an inevitable demise with Katniss helpless to intervene will always be one of the most brutal scenes in the core Hunger Games movies.

Ampert's death in Sunrise on the Reaping is especially cruel, as he's effectively marked for death well before the 50th Hunger Games even begin. This is because Ampert is the son of Beetee, a former victor. After Beetee was caught with plans to disrupt the Capitol's communications systems, his punishment was Ampert being reaped and Beetee being forced to mentor his own son.

Even so, Ampert still helped Haymitch during the Games with Beetee's plan to sabotage the arena. However, Ampert is ultimately attacked by a horde of vicious mutt squirrels, with Haymitch unable to save the young boy despite his best efforts. Not only is it one of the most horrifying mutt deaths, but it's a prime example highlighting the greater context of President Snow's endless cruelty.

Mags Flanagan's sacrifice during the second Quarter Quell is one of the most selfless and tragic moments in Catching Fire. When the poisonous fog threatens to envelop the unified tributes, the elderly Mags recognizes her inability to keep up with the others.

Mags was effectively a surrogate mother to Finnick Odair, having been his mentor when he was the youngest to ever win the Games. Mags also volunteered and took Annie Cresta's place during the uniqie victor's reaping for the 75th Hunger Games' Quarter Quell.

As such, Finnick was determined to save Mags and was carrying her on his back, just barely staying ahead of the toxic fog. However, Mags ends up willingly entering the fog after kissing Finnick goodbye. Removing herself from the board, Mags' sacrifice helped ensure that the younger tributes had better odds of survival.

Sejanus Plinth is one of the few characters in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes who recognizes the cruelty of the fairly new Hunger Games and wants to do something about the Capitol's treatment of the Districts. However, it's his compassion and decision to help District 12 rebels that makes him a major threat to the government, as well as to the ambitions of his best friend, young Coriolanus Snow.

After secretly recording Sejanus' intentions to help the rebellion, Snow betrays Sejanus and sends the evidence to the Capitol. This leads to Plinth's arrest and hanging, with jabberjays perfectly mimicking his cries to his mother after his death. Not only that, but Sejanus' father ends up treating Snow like a son and names him his heir for being "such a good friend" to his son, supporting his education and rise to power (never knowing the major hand Snow had in Sejanus' death), thereby making his demise that much more devastating.

While the deaths of his mother and brother in a fire were horrible, Lenore Dove's death is arguably the most brutal consequence of Haymitch's victory in the 50th Hunger Games, and one of the most devastating in either of The Hunger Games' prequel films.

Having completely destroyed Haymitch's life after the Games, Snow orchestrates the poisoning of gumdrops that were eaten by the love of Haymitch's life, having wrongly assumed the candies were from Haymitch himself. Helpless to do anything but watch Lenore Dove die in his arms, her death is the start of Haymitch's lifetime of grief and isolation, refusing to let anyone get close to him for fear that Snow would kill them next while constantly drinking in a desperate attempt to numb the pain and forget.

Maysilee Donner's death is easily one of the most emotionally devastating moments near the end of the 50th Hunger Games in Sunrise on the Reaping. Having joined Haymitch as two of the last tributes left standing, the two tributes from 12 had a genuine bond as allies and their shared determination to defy the Capitol. However, Maysilee was killed by a flock of flamingo-like bird mutts with razor-sharp beaks the novel confirms were designed to target her specifically and ignore Haymitch, yet another punishment from Snow to make him suffer.

With Maysilee being the third and final tribute to die in Haymitch's arms after Lou Lou and Ampert, the lengths Snow goes to punish Haymitch for his defiance of the Capitol can not be understated. Maysilee's death is particularly cruel, especially considering how it was shown via the Capitol's coverage, with careful editing and narration framing Haymitch as a selfish coward.

Maysilee's death is made even worse during her funeral back at District 12, with a traumatized Haymitch mistaking her twin sister Merrilee as Maysilee herself. Lastly, knowing that Katniss and Peeta later watch footage of her death and Haymitch's "victory" in Catching Fire makes her loss even more significant and impactful.

The youngest tribute from District 12 during Sunrise on the Reaping, it's incredibly tragic and cruel that 13-year-old Louella McCoy never even makes it to the Hunger Games' arena. Having been Haymitch's childhood friend from District 12, the duo promised to have each other's backs. However, the horses during the tributes' chariot parade were spooked by fireworks thrown from the audience. Mass mayhem ensued with Haymitch and Louella's chariot slamming into another. While Haymitch was thrown free, Louella was dragged under the flipped-over chariot before suffering a lethal head injury.

Carrying Louella's body to Snow, an angered Haymitch sarcastically applauds the debacle with a slow clap that effectively puts him in the President's crosshairs. However, what makes her death so much worse is that the Capitol refuses to even acknowledge it.

Shortly after the botched parade, Snow has Louella replaced with an abducted lookalike from District 11 who'd been traumatized and brainwashed to believe herself to be Louella, though the rest of the District 12 tributes chose to call her Lou Lou. On the whole, the Capitol erasing Louella's existence is arguably just as bad and even more disturbing than the death itself. To make matters worse, Haymitch fails to protect Lou Lou in the arena after she's poisoned by toxic flowers early on in the Games.

Without a doubt, Finnick Odair's Mockingjay death is one of the most shocking losses in the entire Hunger Games franchise. After surviving the 75th Hunger Games and becoming a key member of the rebellion at District 13, Finnick finally marries fellow victor Annie Cresta, one of the rare moments of happiness in the franchise's final Mockingjay films.

However, Finnick's future is brutally robbed during the mission to assassinate Snow when he falls into a horde of horrifying lizard-humanoid mutts after helping Katniss and the others escape the sewer tunnels below the Capitol. Katniss is then forced to detonate an explosive device to cover the rest of their team's escape and prevent the mutts from dragging away. Overall, there's a wide consensus that Finnick's death is one of the most devastating considering just how close he was to having his happy ending with Annie.​​​​​​​

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3368. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#3367. The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’

Rita Coburn‘s “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is an extraordinary documentary about an extraordinary man, a film that spans nearly 100 years in two hours, yet never feels rushed or superficial. In her storytelling, Coburn shares with her subject a talent for distilling complex ideas and expressing them with force and clarity; the result is a movie that fully honors the breadth and depth of Du Bois’ achievements as a groundbreaking Black writer, historian, and activist.

One of Coburn’s most potent tools in this regard is the music by composer Kathryn Bostic, who previously collaborated with the director on “Marian Anderson: The Whole World in Her Hands.” Bostic incorporates a wide array of styles and influences in her score, which references the various types of music Du Bois encountered and appreciated as a Black intellectual but isn’t beholden to them; as evocative of Bach and American folk music as it is of 19th-century spirituals and Asian motifs, it’s the sonic equivalent of Du Bois’ literary works. Related Stories ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner 26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’

The scope of the project required Bostic to come at the material from multiple angles and perspectives. “Rita and I talked about what types of touchstones we needed to define the narrative musically,” Bostic told IndieWire. “There was the regional touchstone, the era-specific touchstone, the interior emotional aspects that we wanted to heighten with music. Then there’s always the discovery process as you begin to create.”

For Bostic, that discovery process is one of the most exciting aspects of film composing. While she had a number of reference points as she began work on the score, she soon found herself following intuition to take them in different directions than initially intended. “There’s always what I call the hands-on-the-clay moment,” Bostic said. “You have your list, and you have your frame of reference, but the process is fluid.”

According to Coburn, Bostic’s ability to bring a historical perspective to her scores made her an ideal collaborator for the film. “Kathryn pulled from the region of Great Barrington [where Du Bois was born] as well as New York in that time period, and then what was happening with the African-American community that Du Bois was entering,” Coburn said. “There wasn’t gospel then, so you were looking at a small group of Black people going to the churches there in New England. What were they listening to, and therefore what was he listening to?”

Bostic drew on the music of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, a Black a capella ensemble that inspired Du Bois, but then moved in a completely different direction to explore his time in Berlin, when he encountered and fell in love with classical music. She also incorporated Wolof music from Senegal and the Gambia in collaboration with Coburn’s daughter, who studied classical music and worked in the music department on “Rebel with a Cause.”

“She found a Senegalese professor online who worked with her so she could sing the Wolof,” Coburn said. “Kathryn and I agreed that we had to put the Wolof in the film because it connects Du Bois to his Ghanaian roots. But we had to find it, and we wanted it to be as authentic as possible.”

For Bostic, the challenge was taking an audience from 2026 and presenting the music in a way that would recreate the way in which Du Bois experienced it over a hundred years earlier. “There’s the historic arc of the times, as well as what he’s experiencing emotionally,” Bostic said. In the places where her score was informed by spirituals and the work of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, the composer tried to tie the emotional subtext to the context in which she knew Du Bois was consuming the music.

“When he went to Fisk University, his mother had recently died,” Bostic said. “So that music was a wellspring for his grieving, and I think that depth of sorrow and the catharsis that resulted from that sorrow inspired the sort of deep self-reflection that became such a deep part of who he was. That self-reflection led to a basic decency and humanity, and even now I think of him as being light years ahead of people in the way he embodied justice. I want to shine a light on that.”

Coburn felt a similar sense of purpose, especially since the more she dug into Du Bois’ life the more she realized how relevant his insights were to America in 2026. “He speaks to this current time,” Coburn said, adding that the importance of Du Bois’ work gave her own work a sense of urgency and responsibility. “I knew that it might be 20 or 30 years before we get another Du Bois documentary. I hope not, but I looked at his life and knew that I had to do the best job that I could. We did everything we could for Du Bois because we felt he had done everything he could for us.”

The greatness of “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is that it brings the viewer into Du Bois’ perspective as his world view continues to expand over a 95-year life, and the music is a major part of that subjectivity.

“Kathryn understands that music is a character in any documentary, and her music embodies the character of W.E.B. Du Bois,” Coburn said. “ In the music, we had to grow with him. We had to expand with him. We had to see that his love of Rembrandt and his understanding of classical music, of music that came from an Asian culture, that all of that was important to him. We were catching up with him, and he was driving us.”

“W.E.B. DuBois: Rebel with a Cause” is currently streaming on the PBS app and website.

#3366. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

#3365. 10 Action Video Games That Are Bangers From Start to Finish

When it comes to video games, some of the most popular have always been the likes of action/adventure titles. Video games provide a great escape for the player. Giving them the chance to be an action hero, swinging around New York City, stealing cars, shooting up bad guys, or becoming the samurai of their dreams makes them as popular as they've become.

Like any genre of any medium, though, there are some games that most certainly stand out among the others. This isn't to say that they're better than all the rest—there are too many games to make such an objective statement—but there are some certified bangers that come to mind when the discussion of action video games begins.

This wonderful series by Rocksteady Studios is known as one of the best superhero video game franchises of all time, and for very good reason. A lot of those reasons were either expanded upon from the first game, or established in the second title, Batman: Arkham City. This is known as one of the best superhero games out there, and has gone down in history for it.

Batman: Arkham City is well-known for the common notion that it makes you truly feel like Batman (Kevin Conroy). The gameplay mechanics are very well-executed, and the story is thrilling from start to finish. Not to mention, the return of Kevin Conroy as Batman and Mark Hamill as Joker is a huge win and makes this truly feel like some of the many definitive versions of the characters.

If there's one thing PlayStation is excellent at, it's having some amazing console-exclusive titles. One of the best of recent years is none other than Horizon Zero Dawn. Following the hunter known as Aloy (Ashly Burch), Horizon Zero Dawn takes players on a journey of trying to discover the truth about the hunter's origins, and, in turn, the world around her itself.

This project takes place in a post-apocalyptic setting, but not in the manner of another PlayStation exclusive, The Last of Us. The landscape of Horizon Zero Dawn is wide, vast, and filled with high-technology—machine creatures that are now the apex predators, to be exact. The combat—using Aloy's hunting skills and weapons—is wonderful, and such a blast to play. Not to mention, this new world is such a joy to explore and keeps the players actively wanting to discover more about it via the story and the open-world nature of the title.

When it comes to action, there are few that bring the amount that Hades does. That's because the entire point of the game is, well, action. While there is a story to Hades, the game, at its heart, is a rougelike dungeon crawler title that puts the player against hoards and rooms upon rooms of foes to face as the son of Hades (Logan Cunningham), Zagreus (Darren Korb), attempts to escape the Underworld.

Players will die but, every time they begin anew, they can spend their hard-earned resources to level up and go at it again with new powers. The method to the madness of Hades is failing, trying again, failing, and going until the player finally makes it through. It is an absolute thrill ride the entire way through.

While Sega is most known for the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise, they have another video game series that is widely beloved, Yakuza. The best game in said series is none other than Yazuka 0. The Yakuza series is a great time, and the way it brings together gritty crime drama with some hilarious comedy that keeps the players on their toes.

As stated, the best of the best, Yakuza 0, brings all of these things to the table and enhances them. It follows two stories simultaneously, and that really helps in keeping the players invested. The combat mechanics are phenomenal and the true, main highlight of the game. Yakuza 0 is truly the perfect example of how to make an incredible Yazkua game.

While the recent God of War games are easily some of the best PlayStation titles in recent years, if fans of action want something in the series to seriously deliver on that, they need to look no further than God of War II. This sequel truly delivers on action, spectacle, and fun gameplay. It has a blockbuster-level story that is engaging for the entire runtime.

Not to forget, the players get to take on the gods of Olympus. Kratos (Terrence "T.C." Carson) is out for blood, and he is going to stop at nothing to get it. This allows players to experience some serious spectacle as they fight their way through Olympus and take down the gods. It's a ride filled with intensity till the very end and worth playing every second.

Much like Batman: Arkham City, Insomniac Games' hit title, Marvel's Spider-Man, is well-regarded because of how much it makes the player truly feel like Spider-Man (Yuri Lowenthal). The swinging physics/mechanics are stellar, and easily some of the best in any Spider-Man game ever. Swinging mechanics are so much more important to a Spider-Man game than one would realize on paper. For quite some time, Spider-Man 2's video game was known to have the best.

Many consider it one of the best modern superhero video games of all time. The execution of Marvel's Spider-Man was done with grace and prowess. This reimagining of the Spider-Man world—where Peter Parker is older, experienced, and facing off with enemies he's never faced before—is so well-done, and it's a fan-favorite Spider-Man universe. Playing Marvel's Spider-Man truly does make the player feel like Spider-Man, and, alongside that, has an astounding story.

There are a few things in this life that will always be cool: cowboys, superheroes, spacemen, and . . . samurais. A modern game that might genuinely capture the samurai vibe the best is none other than 2020's Ghost of Tsushima. If there's one thing that can describe this game, it's that it is vastly cinematic. It feels like players are playing through a classic samurai film.

Playing the ever-gorgeous Ghost of Tsushima feels like playing through a movie in all the best ways. The camera, shot framing, battles, and more all make this story amazing to experience. The melee combat is borderline perfect. Sword duels and other action feel so natural and exhilarating to play—it's genuinely difficult to put this amazing game down.

2016's Doom is about as action-packed as it gets. It is a literal non-stop space adventure that has players firing bullets of all kinds into horrifying monsters. Doom rewards players for being aggressive and jumping straight into action, rather than strategy. There is always a battle or chase going down, and it never stops being abundantly exciting.

But players aren't just firing the same kind of gun the entire time—no, there is a gigantic arsenal of weapons players will have the choice to utilize throughout the entire game. Just as importantly, the score behind the action is one of the best action game scores of all time. Composed by the legendary Mick Gordon, everything that is great about Doom is enhanced by Gordon's excellent work.

Another sword-wielding adventure—reminiscent of Ghost of Tsushima—from recent years that is phenomenal is the ever-thrilling Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. Taking place in the late-1500s, this 2019 adventure follows a shinobi named Sekiro (Daisuke Namikawa and Noshir Dalal), players get to step into the shoes of an incredible swordsman as he goes on a journey to rescue his captured lord, Kuro (Miyuki Sato and Amber Hood).

Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice is everything a typical FromSoftware game—Dark Souls, Bloodborne, and Elden Ring—is, in all the best ways. It truly challenges the player in ways other FromSoftware titles don't. It also has a setting unlike the others, too, being set in 1500s Japan. It is so distinct, vast, and exciting that it feels like a must-play for those who love some good sword combat . . . even if it has the classic tough FromSoftware difficuly.

There is absolutely no question that Grand Theft Auto VI is the biggest game of the decade—maybe even the last two decades. People have been waiting for this game for so long that the cultural impact has been increasing little by little every year, exploding in one great release this year. Ask anyone who's played it, and they'll most likely say, "It was worth the wait."

This game is truly something special. It has attention to detail unlike any other, gorgeous visuals, skilled performances, groundbreaking mechanics across the board, and a wonderful story at the core of it all. There are dozens of reasons to love this game, but one of the main highlights are the action sequences—of which there are plenty. Robberies, assassinations, gunfights, etc. bring Grand Theft Auto VI to the top of the "best of all time" list.

The Ma’tok staff (commonly known as a staff weapon) was the Jaffa’s weapon of choice. It is designed to fire bolts of plasma, with a range of 50-60 meters. The intensity of the blasts, which are powered by a Naquadah generator, can be adjusted so it can stun a human or blast through rock.

The Serpent Guard was made up of Apophis’s most trusted Jaffa and for centuries they were dedicated to serving him.

That began to change when Apophis’s First Prime, Teal’c, turned on him and joined SG-1. The replica helmet was digitally sculpted, based on careful study of the original props. #3362. Watch the ‘Project Hail Mary’ VFX Supervisor Explain Why Having Puppeteers on Set Was Worth All the Extra Work

The making of “Project Hail Mary” was a miracle on par with the outer space rescue mission that Ryan Gosling is tasked with pulling off. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s bestselling novel manages to be epic without ever losing its intimacy, as Gosling traverses the galaxy and saves the world with only a very lovable rock acting alongside him. The final product was a complicated blend of practical effects, on-set puppetry, and a healthy dose of VFX magic.

Incorporating so many production elements creates more work for all involved. The puppetry team lead by James Ortiz had to fit into very small spaces, which frequently meant they showed up in the frames. Visual Effects Production Supervisor Mag Sarnowska and her team were tasked with removing all of the puppeteers. But as she explained during the VFX panel at IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables, it was a small price to pay for the way it enhanced Gosling’s acting performance. Related Stories The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’ ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner

“It was so good to have James and his puppeteers, which we called Rocketeers,” Sarnowska said. “It was great to have them there, but it did not work out sometimes. Our sets were really, really tiny. Having five people there to puppet Rocky was hard sometimes. But to everyone’s point, having something there in the frame was so helpful, especially for Ryan to act to. The eyeline? That’s a real thing. Even though our Rocky didn’t have eyes, a person’s brain makes it easier to figure out where the eyes would be just by having that constant relation between Rocky and Ryan.”

Sarnowska — who will share the Innovation Award at the IndieWire Honors with Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, and Paul Lambert — explained that having a real reference point for VFX sequences is what ultimately makes the most effects-heavy sequences feel real.

“In Ryan’s space, he has to be in the xenonite glass, so having reflections, adding the glass, it was a lot of work,” she said. “But having that real thing, having that reference, even if we had to replace it, that was so important. Because we knew what Rocky would look like.”

More coverage from our Craft Roundtables can be found here.
