#3359. The 25 Best Video Games of All Time, Ranked

Especially compared to the likes of literature, theater, and film, whose histories go back over 100 years of history, video games are a much newer artform of creative expression that is still taking shape and evolving year by year. Still, the medium has had an undeniable growth since the early days of arcade shooters and 8-bit graphics, as games are able to tell rich and powerful stories all while being more immersive than any other artform. Especially with Grand Theft Auto VI's recent record-breaking release further cementing video games as the dominant entertainment medium of the modern age, it places an even greater legacy on the games designated as the greatest of all time.

What makes for a truly exceptional video game experience is going to vary and differ from each individual person, as there is no truly 100% correct list of the greatest video games of all time. For the sake of this list, the entries are a collection of games that consistently stand out and come up in conversation not just because of their high quality, but because of the standards they set when they released and their influence on the entire medium. Still, this only scratches the surface of exceptional video games that have been released since the inception of the industry.

While many people may think of the long-running television franchise or even the original comic when it comes to The Walking Dead, gamers will immediately sing the praises of Telltale's legendary point-and-click adventure game. An original story set in the comic book universe, the episodic game set a new standard for emotional storytelling and writing in video games, with a rich narrative influenced by player choice that amplifies the greatest strengths of Robert Kirkman's original series.

With stylish cell-shaded graphics and approachable gameplay simple enough for even casual gamers to enjoy and get wrapped up in the story, Telltale's The Walking Dead does a great job of making its central story as engaging and impactful as possible. While Telltale has continued the story with an array of subsequent sequels and continuing story, it's the original run of 5 episodes that made such a massive impact on audiences as one of the most poignant and beautiful gaming experiences of all time.

In the early days of 8-bit video games, the platformer genre reigned supreme as the most widely popular style of gaming, with no platformer franchise being as popular or immediately recognizable as Super Mario Bros. While the original NES classic is exceptional enough as it is, the brilliance and timeless appeal of the Mario franchise wouldn't be fully realized until Super Mario Bros. 3, which almost 40 years later is still one of the best 2d platformers ever made.

The game absolutely perfects the feeling and smooth controls required of a platformer of the era, being leaps and bounds ahead of its contemporaries in terms of precision and game feel. This is all on top of the overwhelming creativity in terms of the game's level designs and power-ups that truly bring the wild chaos of the Mario world to life. This classic platformer still stands as the absolute best game released on the Nintendo Entertainment System.

A striking monolith of the action-adventure genre from Team Ico, PlayStation 2 classic Shadow of the Colossus has stood as one of the quintessential examples of games as serious art ever since its release. The game features staggering visuals and a gargantuan sense of scale, seeing the player have to face off against various massive creatures across the land with the goal of resurrecting a young woman. Through traversing the world on horse and by foot, its exceptional visuals and minimalist design come together to create a defining gaming experience.

Especially in an era where action adventure gaming was continuously getting louder and more abrasive with its gameplay and visuals, the slow and methodical approach that Shadow of the Colossus took made the game that much more striking and memorable to 2000s gamers. It truly felt ahead of its time in terms of being an interactive work of art, with something meaningful and sorrowful to say in its storytelling instead of pure entertainment.

One of the premiere masterpieces of the PlayStation brand and one of the first games that come to mind for many when considering games that actively go for a cinematic feel, The Last of Us is one of the defining gaming masterpieces of the 2010s. It tells a dark post-apocalyptic story that primarily focuses on the loss of humanity at large, paralleling the unlikely connection that fosters between a smuggler who lost his daughter and a young girl who has only known this apocalyptic world.

While the emotional and groundbreaking storytelling is the primary element that people praise about The Last of Us, the core stealth-centric action gameplay is also worthy of praise, as it gets the player engaged and immersed in this heightened world where anything can go wrong. The game was also for many a massive leap forward in terms of technical craft in visuals, pushing the PlayStation 3 to its limits and ushering in a new age of realism in video games.

One of the great advents of gaming as an artform becoming more accessible in the digital era is that many more independent game developers are able to bring their visions to life, with a wide array of indie game masterpieces being released in the 21st century. One of the most defining and culturally dominant indie games has been Undertale, Toby Fox's quaint and quirky mixture of RPGs like Earthbound and bullet hell games like Touhou Project.

More than anything else, Undertale thrives thanks to its overwhelming charm and ingenuity, utilizing simplistic visuals and dynamic gameplay to create an experience that consistently delights and surprises the player. It certainly has a goofy tongue-in-cheek tone, satirizing many tropes of RPGs and video games as a whole, but there are also a lot of immaculate character writing and exceptional secrets that make Undertale one of the most influential indie games of all time.

An icon of the metroidvania genre so influential that the very genre is in part coined after its exceptional non-linear design, Castlevania: Symphony of the Night is the undeniable high point of a franchise that has delivered gaming greatness ever since the early days of 8-bit consoles. The game originally sold poorly due to being a 2D game released on a console that famously was at the forefront of early 3D gaming, the original PlayStation, but word of mouth about its quality transformed Symphony of the Night into one of gaming's greatest sleeper hits.

The game famously utilized a non-linear approach to the classic concept of exploring Dracula's Castle, allowing the player all sorts of freedom in the order in which they explore the castle and progress through the story. Combined with an incredibly addictive gameplay loop that has the player actively feel their character grow and get stronger as they play, Symphony of the Night has been the standard for non-linear metroidvanias for nearly 3 decades.

The Legend of Zelda series has continuously released some of the most important and widely influential adventures ever made, dating back 40 years of groundbreaking video game experiences. The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild is the best-selling game in the series, as it completely reinvented and redefined what a Zelda game could be in the modern age and becoming one of the all-time greatest open world games.

Breath of the Wild was a game defined by its sense of pure freedom as an open world adventure, giving the player more control in terms of the order that they go about events compared to any other adventure game at the time, even able to go right to the final boss from the very beginning. Combined with a dynamic physics system and an overwhelming amount of charm and attention to detail, Breath of the Wild has been the quintessential Nintendo masterpiece of the past 10 years.

A story-based RPG that utilizes tabletop mechanics as the centric for its gameplay and setting, Disco Elysium is a masterclass of narrative and storytelling in the medium of video games. It's very abstract as far as RPGs are concerned, having very little combat and instead utilizing its RPG mechanics as skill checks for various actions and dialogue trees, much like a tabletop game would. This classic gameplay loop makes for one of the most immersive and limitless stories in gaming history, branching out into a wide array of different possibilities entirely dependent on player choice.

Its prospects as an indie game allow Disco Elysium not to hold back in terms of the symbolic themes and messaging of its story, commending on so many different aspects of life, government, and ideology in a game rich with perfectly written dialogue across the board. Disco Elysium is one of the greatest works of art that modern gaming has to offer, and is an absolute must-play for anyone who appreciates a great story in video games.

Once video games started to get larger in scale and complexity, the turn-based RPG inspired by games like Dungeons & Dragons became one of the best showcases for an immersive, long-lasting adventure; with Square being one of the best studios for RPGs in the classic era. One of several iconic Square RPGs was Chrono Trigger, a time traveling adventure sporting character designs from Dragon Ball creator Akira Toriyama that quickly became heralded as an RPG masterpiece.

The game has an immediately engaging story, following a group of adventurers from across time who work together to prevent a global catastrophe. While many other RPGs of the 20th century would largely focus on classic fantasy archetypes and elements, Chrono Trigger acted as this sprawling mixture of fantasy and sci-fi elements that was incredibly unique for the time. Mixed with immaculate storytelling and a perfect original soundtrack, to create one of the first times that a game fully enthralled and enchanted players as a complete experience.

Outer Wilds is one of the greatest examples of how, even in the modern age of video games, there are exciting and groundbreaking original concepts still being made that completely reshape and redefine what a video game can be. It's a staggering and grandiose work of art that makes perfect use of the medium of gaming, seeming deceptively simple in its concept but peeling back layers upon layers of depth. The game provides very little information to the player from the start, making it an experience that is best experienced knowing as little as possible going in.

What can be mentioned is the game's base premise, as it sees the player exploring a planetary system that is stuck in a 22-minute time loop that ends in the entire system being destroyed when its sun goes supernova. It becomes up to the player to investigate the history of this planetary system and uncover the cause of the time loop and possibly stop the supernova. Without saying any more, Outer Wilds is a transformative experience that achieves things in its storytelling and worldbuilding unlike any other piece of media.

#3353. No Sci-Fi Series Does Dystopian Worldbuilding Better Than Netflix's 34-Episode Masterpiece

Worldbuilding is a vital component of any sci-fi series, but especially when it comes to the dystopian subgenre. These shows can't just rely on a tyrannical villain or hideous monster to chill viewers; the story's reality needs to be terrifying by itself. George Orwell's 1984 isn't the touchstone of dystopian storytelling because Big Brother is a great antagonist, but because the alternate future Orwell describes is vividly and unapologetically unsettling.

The elites of dystopian TV operate on a similar premise. The Handmaid's Tale crafts a devastatingly miserable political landscape, while 12 Monkeys blends dystopian tropes with mind-bending sci-fi to glorious effect. There isn't exactly a shortage of great dystopian TV shows out there, but there is one standing head and shoulders above the rest.

Running for seven seasons (and a film!) across both Channel 4 and Netflix, Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror has pierced pop culture like a spear through Brie. The phrase "like Black Mirror" has taken on a life of its own as a way to describe social and technological developments that give us the heebie-jeebies. That never would have happened unless Black Mirror had a knack for creating dystopian futures that haunt us, but the show's worldbuilding prowess is even more impressive than you realize.

The vast majority of sci-fi shows, especially those dwelling within the dystopian realm, are serialized in nature, meaning they enjoy the advantage of building fictional worlds across multiple episodes or seasons. In theory, more time means more detail, and more detail means a more fully-formed dystopia develops.

It's a credit to Charlie Brooker that Black Mirror achieves a more powerful effect despite telling separate stories in every episode. Each installment has only an hour or so to convey its dystopian setting, often using only a handful of characters and locations, and yet Black Mirror's vision of the future is almost always more emotionally affecting than a multi-season rivals with one story running all the way through.

Black Mirror boasts an uncanny ability to weave large dystopian worlds using smaller, more personal narratives. "Metalhead" never explains why civilization has collapsed or where the robot dogs came from, but Bella perfectly captures the desperation of humanity's survivors. Maxine Peake's performance gets across the hope, the fear, and the ruthlessness of the episode's dystopia better than most shows manage within an entire season, and it's those emotions that embed themselves deep into viewers' minds.

"Plaything" takes the opposite approach, chronicling the very moment human society falls into the post-apocalyptic hands of a sentient computer program, acting as an origin story for a dystopia we never truly get to see. Once again, however, the story orbits entirely around the emotional impact of these events upon one man: Peter Capaldi's Cameron.

Black Mirror's worldbuilding is head and shoulders above other sci-fi shows because instead of asking 'how did the world end?' it asks 'how was the life of this one specific individual destroyed?' For viewers, that personal touch offers the more harrowing experience, even when compared against long-running shows that contextualize their dystopias in painstaking detail. It's telling that, going back to 1984, Orwell's book essentially does the same thing with Winston. It's the POV character study that makes 1984 so unnerving.

Black Mirror also honors the longstanding horror rule that what you don't see is scarier than what you do, and each of its dystopian episodes carry a sense of unseen mystery. Indeed, it's the same unseen mystery every time: the vague suggestion that different parts of Black Mirror are secretly connected.

"Plaything" being a sequel to "Bandersnatch" creates a sense of impending doom. And the notion that the post-apocalypse from "Metalhead" can be traced back to Michael Callow's ham sandwich in "The National Anthem" creates a grim sense of inevitable destruction across the entire series. It's almost like a deeper, darker conspiracy is bubbling beneath the show's surface. It's a nagging, worrying sensation that only makes Black Mirror's dystopian universe even harder to shake out of our heads when an episode's end credits roll.

#3352. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3350. Disney Officially Decides the Fate of James Cameron’s ‘Avatar 4’

It's a fairly ridiculous position for James Cameron to find himself in when making almost $1.5 billion at the worldwide box office is considered something of a disappointment, but that's the problem with having directed three of the highest-grossing movies in the history of cinema. Having spent much of the last two decades on Pandora, Cameron has been increasingly vocal about his desire to make other movies, with his planned adaptation of Joe Abercrombie's The Devils and his long-gestating Hiroshima project among those he's particularly keen to get behind the camera for. Despite Avatar: Fire and Ash making around $1.48 billion worldwide, that's still considerably less than the $2.32 billion made by Avatar: The Way of Water, and Cameron has spoken about wanting to bring down both the cost of making the movies and the amount of time he spends making them. Executive producer Rae Sanchini, however, told Inverse earlier this year that preparations for the next two movies were already underway, with the team working on budgets, scheduling, and technology.

The cast of Fire and Ash includes Sam Worthington (Horizon: An American Saga) as Jake Sully, Zoe Saldaña (Guardians of the Galaxy) as Neytiri, Sigourney Weaver (Alien) as Kiri, Stephen Lang (Don't Breathe) as Miles Quaritch, Oona Chaplin (Game of Thrones) as Varang, Britain Dalton as Lo'ak, Jack Champion (Scream VI) as Spider, and Bliss as Tuk.

Avatar 4 remains scheduled for December 21, 2029, with Avatar 5 dated for December 19, 2031. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

#3349. Garmin Watches Are up to 44% Off in This Early Black Friday Sale

Thanksgiving is a full week away, but early Black Friday sales are already here. I've been keeping an eye on all the best fitness trackers and smartwatch deals so that you can snag the best possible price from now until the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

If you're looking for a sports watch, Garmin sets the standard. Right now, my favorite Garmin, the Forerunner 970, is $100 off, bringing the price down to $649.99. While this is one of the best running watches money can buy, I know it's a far cry from a budget option when you're shopping deals this holiday season. Luckily, there are plenty of more Garmin options seeing record-low prices right now. Here are more of the best Black Friday deals on Garmin watches that I've seen so far.

The 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 is 249.99 (down from $449.99). The 1.2-inch color AMOLED display makes the screen more readable in bright daylight conditions, and battery life is best-in-class—a must for those going off-grid.

For most color combinations, the Garmin Fenix 8 is discounted 25% to $749.99 (down from $999.99). If you opt for slate gray with a black band, you can snag this premium watch for as low as $719.89. While this is last year's model, it's a perfectly solid option if you don't specifically need the titanium case or the latest mapping engine in the latest Fenix 9 Pro.

The Garmin Forerunner 265 is $299.99 (down from $449.99). Although it isn't the latest and greatest anymore, this is still a fan favorite among Garmin users. It's a step above entry-level options, with dual-band GPS, power meter compatibility, and advanced analytics (like training status).

The Garmin Venu 4 is $449 (down from $549). If you're looking for something not so rugged or sport-specific, the Venu 4 is one of Garmin's best daily health options. It has an AMOLED touchscreen, stainless steel bezel, Gorilla Glass 3 face, and a speaker and microphone that allow it to take voice calls if your phone is within range. It is still a great sports watch, coming with training status, training readiness, and Garmin Coach.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

Yes, Garmin is one of the best brands when it comes to rugged sports watches and fitness trackers. The Forerunner line, especially, is a go-to pick for accurate and reliable GPS tracking for runners.
